variants.reconstruction:
%n [...] ... waršūtim?
#note: The form is usually read as @akk{wa-ar#-ba#-ti}, taken by von Soden (@bib{RN2720@ 1464 s.v. warbum}) as a form of @i{arbu} “öde”. This, however, would be the only attestation of this already scarcely attested lemma with initial @i{w}. As von Soden himself (@bib{RN2720@66b s.v. arbu(m) 2}) suggests, @i{arbu} might actually be a secondary form of @i{harbu} I with the same meaning. Therefore, an original initial @i{w} is rather unlikely. Judging from the photograph in @bib{RN262@404}, the sign in question looks a lot like BA, but might be slightly damaged ŠU. In any case, the lower horizontal wedge excludes KU, which would allow for a reading @i{warkûti} “the later ones”.

variants.reconstruction:
%n [...] ...
#note: @bib{temp_id_4487036324091982@86} has @akk{i-ru-ba-nim}, which would be @i{īrubānim} “they entered”. @bib{RN262@278} reads @akk{i-ib-ka-nim} after collation of the penultimate sign of the line. While she does not translate the passage, the only possible verb to fit her reading would be @i{bakû} “to cry”. As this is not a I/ʾ verb, however, it is unlikely to be written with initial @akk{i-ib}- (see @i{GAG} 28f. §23 d). Keeping in mind this OB graphical convention, only two patterns are probable: a) @i{i}-CV-CV-@i{nim} (i.e. a preterite form of a I/ʾ verb) and b) @i{i-i}C-CV-@i{nim} (i.e. a present form of a I/ʾ and III/voc verb). The passage should be collated anew.
